title: Example — Privacy checks before publishing to GitHub
summary: Review source files, Git history and release artifacts before a first publication or update, without exposing credentials or personal information.
content:
## Purpose and use

A generic example to adapt to your project. Consult it before a commit, push, tag, pull request or release. It supplements project rules; it is neither a security guarantee nor permission to publish. Apply the same checks to private repositories: collaborators and visibility can change.

## 1. Identify what will be published

- Identify the remote repository, branch, commits, tags and release assets. Confirm the intended destination and visibility.
- Inspect changes, staged files and files actually tracked by Git, including hidden files. Useful local checks include `git status --short`, `git diff`, `git diff --cached` and `git ls-files`.
- Check files added by build tools. A `.gitignore` does not untrack files already committed.

## 2. Find information that should remain local

- Credentials: API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, cookies, sessions and credentials inside URLs or connection strings. Include configurations and test fixtures in the review.
- Personal information: private email addresses, local account names, user or build paths, machine identifiers, private network addresses and customer information. Distinguish these values from fictional examples and necessary technical references.
- Local files: `.env` files, databases, personal libraries, backups, logs, exports, editor settings and temporary files. Exclude them from both the repository and the distributed package.
- Documents and images: inspect visible content, metadata, screenshots and examples. Use fictional data for demonstrations.
- Git identity: check authors and email addresses on outgoing commits. If a GitHub noreply address is desired, use the address belonging to that account and configure only this repository. Do not change global Git settings or rewrite existing commits without an explicit request.

## 3. Review history

For the first review, or when no reliable previous review exists, inspect all available history of the branches and tags being published. For an update, inspect every new commit since the last verified state, not only the current files.

Use an available secret scanner, such as Gitleaks, and supplement its results with a project-specific inspection. Assess findings without copying sensitive values into shared reports. A scan with no findings is not proof that nothing has leaked.

## 4. Fix findings without breaking the application

- Replace sensitive values with local configuration or settings supplied by the user. Ship fictional configuration examples only.
- Preserve personal files and local changes. Removing a file from Git does not mean deleting it from disk. Configure exclusions for both Git and the installer.
- Preserve required features, MCP connectors, SDKs, provider names and license notices. A reference to OpenAI, Claude or another provider is not itself a privacy leak.
- If a real secret has already been exposed, inform its owner privately and arrange revocation or rotation. A deletion commit does not remove it from history.
- Do not force-push, rewrite shared history or delete a release without explicit authorization for that operation.

## 5. Review release artifacts

Rebuild binaries from the reviewed source. Inspect the actual contents of archives, executables, installers, symbol files and configuration files: embedded data, unexpected files, metadata and build paths. Reviewing source alone is insufficient. Do not rename an old binary and present it as a new build.

Run checks appropriate to the change and test installation or startup when distributing an executable. Verify the exact list of attached release assets and their hashes. For updates, also verify preservation of user data.

## 6. Decide and report

- Resolve blocking findings before uploading. If a necessary check could not be performed, report the limitation and hold the affected publication until it is resolved or the responsible owner explicitly decides how to proceed.
- Publish only within the authorization already given. This example grants no additional permission.
- Describe concrete product changes in commits, pull requests and release notes. Do not add claims such as “no secrets”, “audit passed” or “clean release”.
- Report privately what was actually inspected, what was corrected, which tests ran, and any remaining limitations or actions. Never copy secrets into the report or claim checks that were not performed.

## Final checklist

- [ ] Publication destination and outgoing files identified.
- [ ] Source, changes and relevant history inspected.
- [ ] Secrets and personal information addressed; local files preserved.
- [ ] Required features, licenses and connectors preserved.
- [ ] Appropriate tests passed; release package inspected when applicable.
- [ ] Publication authorized; release notes describe product changes.
- [ ] Private report accurately reflects the checks performed.
